business_model: Freemium subscription; early access.

Published consumer pricing.

weaknesses: Early-access status; paid-plan adoption and retention are unknown.

business_model: Mobile app with in-app subscriptions.

target_customer: People and caregivers managing medications.
weaknesses: Narrower than full family-care coordination; user-reported public discussion cites subscription cost and manual medication entry as friction.

business_model: No-cost nonprofit platform.

weaknesses: Designed primarily for updates/support rather than comprehensive medical, financial, or task administration.

Free and simple for a support community.

business_model: Employer/health-plan benefit and private paid subscription.
category: care concierge and employee caregiving benefit

Published private-pay plan and employer benefit channel.

business_model: Local private-pay service; some insurance/benefit offsets may apply.

notes: Relevant paid alternative for care-capacity work, not a software competitor. Do not generalize local rates nationally.

strengths: Human service can absorb physical tasks, transportation, and respite.
Local published price examples show existing service spend.
target_customer: Older adults and families purchasing local in-home companion, personal, or dementia care.
weaknesses: Pricing, minimums, and service availability vary by location and care level; local pages require a quote for many arrangements.

business_model: Tiered subscription with optional add-ons and monthly/annual billing choices.
evidence_type: FACT: official pricing/help pages plus limited public review evidence
name: Jobber
negative_feedback: Public reviews mention cost for additional users, routing limitations, feature gaps, and occasional integration issues; sample is not representative.
notes: Relevant direct substitute. Existing reviews include both material admin/cash-flow benefits and complaints, so do not infer broad dissatisfaction.
positioning: Field-service operating system for quoting, scheduling, invoicing, payments, job costing, and client communication.
pricing: FACT: official annual-billed starting prices are US$29/month Core (1 user), US$99/month Connect (includes 5 users), US$149/month Grow (includes 10 users), and US$399/month Plus (includes 15 users). Optional Marketing Suite, AI Receptionist, and Pipeline are listed at US$99, US$29, and US$49/month respectively. Payment-processing fees vary by plan and are not summarized here.
strengths: Published pricing and team-inclusive tiers.
Direct coverage of all three PER-003 workflows.
Official terms allow a no-commitment monthly option.
target_customer: Local field-service teams, including 6-15-user teams.
weaknesses: Advanced job costing and automation are higher-tier features.
Additional functionality can require add-ons; buyer must verify total cost.

business_model: Subscription with plan recommendation by industry, team size, and goals; third-party offerings and payment services may be additional.
evidence_type: FACT: official pricing/terms plus limited public review evidence
name: Housecall Pro
negative_feedback: One public review cites invoicing limitations as the business grew; isolated feedback does not establish a broad pattern.
notes: Direct substitute across all three Problems. Vendor's stated revenue/time-saved claims are not treated as independent outcomes.
positioning: All-in-one home-service platform for booking, dispatch, quotes, invoices, payments, pricebooks, job costing, and reviews.
pricing: FACT: official page shows Basic at US$59/month billed annually for one included user and Essentials at US$149/month billed annually in the displayed configuration. Team pricing beyond displayed tiers is dynamic/UNKNOWN and should be quoted. 14-day free trial is advertised.
strengths: Published entry pricing and broad operational workflow coverage.
Targets many PER-003 trades and team-size bands.
target_customer: Home-service businesses from solo operations to teams.
weaknesses: Full team-plan prices are not consistently displayed without configuration.
Review evidence identifies invoice limitations for some growing/property-management use cases.

business_model: Customized per-technician subscription packages plus separately invoiced professional services when ordered.
evidence_type: FACT: official pricing/onboarding and investor filing plus limited public review evidence
name: ServiceTitan
negative_feedback: Small-business reviews cite complexity, onboarding burden, and fit concerns; these are not prevalence estimates.
notes: Important high-capability incumbent. Its presence validates category spend but does not itself prove a gap for 5-25 employee firms.
positioning: Comprehensive contractor operating platform with dispatch, scheduling, call booking, invoicing, pricebook, mobile estimates, payroll, reporting, and memberships.
pricing: FACT: ServiceTitan publishes Starter, Essentials, and The Works packages and says pricing is per technician, but does not publish dollar prices; quote required. Its public filing says subscription pricing generally depends on package and business size, with professional services separately invoiced when ordered.
strengths: Broad workflow and reporting coverage.
Formal onboarding stages and implementation support are documented.
target_customer: Contractors of varied sizes, including residential, commercial, enterprise, and franchise operations.
weaknesses: Public dollar price, implementation fee, and commitment are UNKNOWN without a quote.
Setup requires discovery, data, pricebook, and accounting preparation.

business_model: Tiered Standard, Pro, and Ultimate subscription with add-ons; request-pricing model.
evidence_type: FACT: official pricing page plus limited public review evidence
name: Workiz
negative_feedback: Review-site evidence includes claimed integration/sync problems and feature limitations; it is not representative.
notes: Direct substitute; opaque dollar pricing limits comparison of the proposed systems-fit gap.
positioning: Field-service platform combining scheduling, jobs, estimates, invoices, payments, communication, route planning, inventory, and lead management.
pricing: FACT: official site lists Standard, Pro, and Ultimate but requires a price request; it advertises a seven-day no-card free trial and says annual subscriptions can save US$400+. Exact monthly price, per-user price, and add-on costs are UNKNOWN from the public page.
strengths: Covers coordination and quote-to-cash workflows in one system.
Public plan structure and free-trial path reduce evaluation friction.
target_customer: Growing, mid-size, and larger field-service teams.
weaknesses: Public dollar pricing is unavailable.
Public review evidence includes sync, connectivity, billing, and reporting complaints.

business_model: Seat-based customized contract; paid migration available; optional premium capabilities and embedded payments.
evidence_type: FACT: official pricing, agreement, payment terms plus limited public review evidence

negative_feedback: A small construction-owner review cites fragmented navigation across estimates, invoices, purchase orders, and services; not representative.

positioning: Configurable field-service platform for scheduling, dispatch, work orders, estimates/invoices, workflow automation, QuickBooks sync, and add-on communications/AI.
pricing: FACT: official pricing page says quotes are customized by team setup and distinguishes full-access and field-only seats. Its public pricing tool displayed US$99 per user, US$125/month for five Engage-phone users, US$25/additional phone user, and US$795 premium support; treat tool values as configuration-dependent. Standard payment terms list 3.00% card, 1.00% ACH, US$0.25 item, US$9 monthly-access, and related fees.
strengths: Explicit field-only versus full-access seat concept.
Documents migration, configuration, and training process.
target_customer: Growing field-service teams needing full-access office and field-only mobile seats.
weaknesses: Customized pricing reduces up-front comparison transparency.
Migration requires customer data preparation; documented integration limitations remain.

business_model: Tiered subscription per seat, with online-payment processing fees varying by payment method.
evidence_type: FACT: official pricing/features plus limited public review evidence
name: Bonsai
negative_feedback: G2 review summaries identify missing features, limited customization, integration issues, and expense concerns; these are not prevalence estimates.
notes: Material direct substitute for both PER-004 Problems. Its broad coverage means a residual paid job must be distinct from an integrated business suite.
positioning: Integrated CRM, proposals, agreements, client portal, projects, time tracking, billing, payments, bookkeeping, rate cards, and budgeting.
pricing: FACT: official pricing lists Basic US$15/month or US$9/month annually; Essentials US$25 or US$19 annually; Premium US$39 or US$29 annually; Elite US$59 or US$49 annually. Payment-fee details vary by method and are not summarized here.
strengths: Directly covers proposal, agreement, project, time, billing, and payment handoffs.
Publishes low-entry single-seat pricing and many scope-of-work/consulting templates.
target_customer: Consultancies, professional services, and project-based businesses; public pricing also shows single-seat plans.
weaknesses: Official onboarding/migration detail is aimed at teams of 10+ users.
The presence of features does not prove scope-control process adoption or reliable workflow configuration.

QuickBooks/Calendly/Zapier integrations and automations on Essentials+

strengths: Directly addresses lead-to-payment and client workflow consolidation.
Starter includes proposals, contracts, invoices, payments, calendar, client portal, and unlimited projects/clients.

weaknesses: Automation and advanced integrations require higher plans.
A review reports calendar-sync conflict and another reports payment-processing inconsistency; fit varies by workflow.

automated workflows, public proposals, Zapier, and bookkeeping integration on Premier

Premier explicitly includes automated workflows, public proposals, scheduling, and integrations.

Official testimonials are vendor-provided and are not independent evidence of typical outcomes.

payment collection, reminders, and document analytics

strengths: Directly supports proposals, approvals, change documentation, contracts, and payment collection.
Business plan explicitly includes approval workflows and CRM integrations.
target_customer: Businesses needing proposals, agreements, e-signatures, approval workflows, and document operations.
weaknesses: Does not itself establish commercial boundaries or ensure a consultant enforces a change process.
Business-level workflows add another subscription and configuration task.

Supports location and virtual-availability filtering.

weaknesses: Does not publish provider pricing, appointment availability, fit, or outcomes.
A directory cannot resolve local supply or owner-specific service selection.

Includes non-training roles relevant to care logistics.

The directory cannot itself supply an appointment or replace professional evaluation.

strengths: Low published entry price relative to reported private-training costs.
Provides remote access and ongoing subscription option.
target_customer: Dog owners seeking self-paced or subscription-based online training content and trainer/community access.
weaknesses: Vendor marketing and testimonials do not establish typical outcomes.
Owner implementation and fit remain necessary; it does not establish local-service availability.

name: Reacpaw
negative_feedback: An App Store reviewer requested medication tracking, editable triggers, route maps, and watch support (OBS-000110); this is an individual feature request, not prevalence evidence.
notes: Material direct substitute for PROB-0010. Its existence and spreadsheet alternatives materially weaken an assumption of an empty tracking market.
positioning: Dedicated app for recording reactivity, reviewing patterns, sharing progress, and managing a shared account.

strengths: Directly addresses logging and household sharing rather than generic note-taking.
Recent releases show continuing product development.
target_customer: Owners who want to log reactive-dog triggers, walks, and longitudinal progress.
weaknesses: Visible App Store review count is small; review requests include more tracking features.
No evidence establishes that owners pay separately for its tracking function or retain use.

business_model: Appointment-based specialty professional service with an initial consultation and follow-up care.

features: Virtual follow-ups for established patients where permitted

negative_feedback: No directly attributable customer dissatisfaction record was used.
notes: Material specialist-service substitute for PROB-0011 and evidence that a higher-need owner segment may face an ongoing, locally constrained service model. No clinical recommendation is implied.
positioning: Specialty practice requiring an in-person initial appointment in Stafford Springs, Connecticut; established-patient follow-ups may occur by Zoom.
pricing: FACT: published initial behavior consultation is US$650, non-refundable, for 60–90 minutes plus history review and written report. The page says ongoing follow-up is necessary; follow-up price is not published. This is one Connecticut practice, not a national rate.
strengths: Published price and defined intake/follow-up workflow make the cost and repeat-support model visible.
Coordinates records with a primary veterinarian and may work with trainers.
target_customer: Pet owners seeking appointment-based specialty behavior consultation in Connecticut, with some follow-up and professional-consultation pathways.
weaknesses: Initial visit is in-person in one Connecticut location; remote access has legal and established-patient constraints.
Price/payment terms and physical travel can be access barriers.

business_model: Consumer subscription; professional program also charges per active client.
evidence_type: FACT: vendor pricing and support materials; individual repository observations for experience limits.

negative_feedback: PER-009 reviews report connection, duplicate-transaction, and manual-correction issues; these are individual reports, not category prevalence evidence (OBS-000127, OBS-000129, OBS-000130).
notes: Material direct substitute for shared visibility in PROB-0012. Existence and household collaboration weaken a generic shared-dashboard gap; it does not establish continuity completeness or target-persona retention.
positioning: Household finance dashboard with collaboration, separate and joint account aggregation, and advisor access.
pricing: FACT: vendor page lists US$99.99/year or US$14.99/month after a seven-day trial; pricing may change.
strengths: Directly supports a whole-household view and collaboration.
Published consumer price and professional-access model.
target_customer: Households wanting a shared view of accounts, spending, budgets, and goals.
weaknesses: All household members have the same full visibility into connected accounts; account-level hiding is not offered.
Does not replace a deliberate credential/document continuity process.

negative_feedback: An attributed App Store review described a primary-account sync failure; this is one review, not prevalence evidence (OBS-000137).

Repository evidence includes a paid user who sought a daily account view (OBS-000135).

weaknesses: A finance dashboard is not a full document, credential, or handoff system.
Repository reviews describe provider-specific synchronization concerns (OBS-000137).

business_model: Consumer subscription.

negative_feedback: No attributable customer complaint was used in this analysis.

Separates shared and private storage rather than requiring full household financial visibility.

A household still must decide what to inventory and maintain.

A single engagement portal can reduce email and folder fragmentation.

It does not serve as a complete household financial system of record.

Covers records and document organization across systems.

No evidence establishes broad target-persona adoption for these two jobs.

business_model: B2B subscription; the reviewed AI add-ons are priced per employee or manager and require qualifying platform packages.

AI meeting notes, summaries, and suggested actions

target_customer: Organizations, managers, and direct-report teams using structured performance and manager-development workflows.
weaknesses: Requires organizational adoption, qualifying platform package, calendar setup, and manager/direct-report participation.
Vendor materials establish capability, not that every manager configures or uses it competently.

target_customer: Organizations operating people-development, performance, and recurring manager/employee meeting workflows.
weaknesses: B2B adoption and organizational configuration are required.
Vendor feature claims do not establish that managers lacking foundational skill or discipline will follow through.

business_model: Practitioner/clinic subscription; patient-facing PhysiApp access is free to patients.
category: clinician exercise-prescription, patient-engagement, and telehealth platform
evidence_type: FACT: official support and pricing materials; repository observation for adequacy.
name: Physitrack / PhysiApp
negative_feedback: Repository evidence: PhysiApp was reported helpful for exercise videos, reminders, comfort logging, and progress tracking (OBS-000174).
notes: Material substitute for clinician-to-athlete program delivery and follow-up in PROB-0015. It reduces any claim that exercise handoff, progress tracking, and patient-clinician messaging require a new athlete tool; it does not prove cross-provider coordination is universal.
positioning: Provider-selected platform for exercise delivery, patient progress and outcome tracking, messaging, and telehealth through PhysiApp.
pricing: FACT: official US pricing page listed US$18.99/practitioner/month or US$227.88/practitioner/year for the standard plan on 2026-09-08. Official support states patients are not charged directly for PhysiApp access.
strengths: Directly covers clinician-to-athlete delivery of a program, progress updates, questions, and telehealth within one workflow.
The pricing/payer model identifies the clinic or practitioner—not the athlete—as purchaser for the clinician coordination layer.
target_customer: Physical therapists, clinics, and their patients.
weaknesses: The reviewed first-party materials do not establish external coach access, clinician-to-coach handoff, or cross-vendor training-plan synchronization.
Absence of a reviewed feature claim is not proof of an unmet paid job or a reason athletes would pay separately.

business_model: B2B2C: employer/health-plan benefit and provider ecosystem; no consumer list price was verified.
category: employer/health-plan digital musculoskeletal care and care-coordination platform
evidence_type: FACT: official care and HingeConnect pages; repository observation for member experience.
name: Hinge Health / HingeConnect
negative_feedback: No attributable Hinge-specific post-adoption coordination failure was found in the repository evidence used here.
notes: Material substitute and negative evidence for a broad "digital and in-person care cannot be coordinated" claim. It cannot be generalized to universal availability or coach-training-plan coordination.
positioning: Digital MSK clinic combining guided exercise, dedicated care teams, virtual care, and coordination with external in-person providers.
pricing: UNKNOWN: no current consumer price was verified. Official pages position access through employers and health plans.
strengths: Directly demonstrates an existing paid/covered model for integrating digital and in-person MSK care, including external-provider coordination.
Repository observation reports insurer-provided Hinge Health coaching, exercise support, sensors, and optional PT as helpful for consistency (OBS-000176).
target_customer: Health plans, employers, members, and participating care providers.
weaknesses: Evidence does not establish that typical recreational athletes access this model or that it coordinates with an athlete’s independent running coach/training app.
It is clinical care, not evidence that a consumer will pay separately for a non-clinical coordination layer.

business_model: Coach and athlete subscriptions; coaches may bundle athlete premium access into their coaching fees.
category: coach-athlete training planning, workout-data, and communication platform
evidence_type: FACT: official coach, messaging, and notification documentation; repository observation for paid-service adequacy.
features: Prehab, rehab, and strength programming support
name: TrainingPeaks
negative_feedback: No attributable TrainingPeaks-specific coordination failure was found in the repository evidence used here.
notes: Material substitute for coach-athlete training execution and communication in PROB-0015. It weakens a broad claim that training changes, activity data, and coach awareness require a new standalone workflow.
positioning: Coach-athlete platform for training plans, activity data, workout comments, notifications, messaging, and device/wearable synchronization.
pricing: FACT: official coach page states athletes pay US$9.92–20/month for Premium depending on billing cadence, and that coaches commonly factor Premium cost into monthly fees. Pricing may change.
strengths: Directly covers coach awareness of training activity, athlete updates, comments, plan execution, and coach-athlete communication.

Vendor materials state it can reduce spreadsheets and switching between training apps; the Scout corpus reports paid coach-supported TrainingPeaks use helping an athlete rebuild after PT (OBS-000164).
target_customer: Endurance coaches, coached athletes, and coach organizations.
weaknesses: The reviewed documentation does not establish clinician access or automated clinical-restriction import.
Its ability to cover training execution does not establish that a separate cross-provider product has a buyer, particularly where a coach can use existing communication/process.
